subject: Physics
question_text:
Answer the following questions regarding earth’s magnetism:
(a) A vector needs three quantities for its specification. Name the three independent quantities conventionally used to specify the earth’s magnetic field.
(b) The angle of dip at a location in southern India is about 18º. Would you expect a greater or smaller dip angle in Britain?
(c) If you made a map of magnetic field lines at Melbourne in Australia, would the lines seem to go into the ground or come out of the ground?
(d) In which direction would a compass free to move in the vertical plane point to, if located right on the geomagnetic north or south pole?
(e) The earth’s field, it is claimed, roughly approximates the field due to a dipole of magnetic moment 8 × 10²² J T⁻¹ located at its centre. Check the order of magnitude of this number in some way.
(f) Geologists claim that besides the main magnetic N-S poles, there are several local poles on the earth’s surface oriented in different directions. How is such a thing possible at all?

mcq_options.option_text: A vector needs three quantities for its specification. Name the three independent quantities conventionally used to specify the earth’s magnetic field.\n
The angle of dip at a location in southern India is about 18º. Would you expect a greater or smaller dip angle in Britain?\n
If you made a map of magnetic field lines at Melbourne in Australia, would the lines seem to go into the ground or come out of the ground?\n

In which direction would a compass free to move in the vertical plane point to, if located right on the geomagnetic north or south pole?\n(e) The earth’s field, it is claimed, roughly approximates the field due to a dipole of magnetic moment 8 × 10²² J T⁻¹ located at its centre. Check the order of magnitude of this number in some way.\n(f) Geologists claim that besides the main magnetic N-S poles, there are several local poles on the earth’s surface oriented in different directions. How is such a thing possible at all?

parts.part_text:
The three independent quantities conventionally used for specifying earth’s magnetic field are:
Magnetic declination,
Angle of dip, and
Horizontal component of earth’s magnetic field.
parts.answer_text: Magnetic declination, Angle of dip, and Horizontal component of earth’s magnetic field.
parts.final_answer: These are the three independent quantities used to specify the earth's magnetic field.

parts.part_text: The angle of dip would be greater in Britain (it is about 70°) than in southern India because the location of Britain on the globe is closer to the magnetic North Pole.
parts.answer_text: The angle of dip is greater in Britain due to its proximity to the magnetic North Pole.
parts.final_answer: Thus, the dip angle is expected to be greater in Britain.

parts.part_text: In a map depicting earth’s magnetic field lines, the field lines at Melbourne, Australia would seem to come out of the ground.
parts.answer_text: The field lines at Melbourne would seem to come out of the ground.
parts.final_answer: Therefore, the lines appear to come out of the ground.

parts.part_text: If a compass is located on the geomagnetic North Pole or South Pole, then the compass will be free to move in the horizontal plane while earth’s field is exactly vertical to the magnetic poles. In such a case, the compass can point in any direction.
parts.answer_text: The compass can point in any direction at the geomagnetic poles.
parts.final_answer: Thus, the compass is free to point in any direction.

parts.part_text: This quantity is of the order of magnitude of the observed field on earth.
parts.answer_text: The magnetic moment is approximately 8 × 10²² J T⁻¹.
parts.final_answer: Hence, it approximates the observed field on earth.

parts.part_text: A magnetised mineral deposit is an example of a local N-S pole.
parts.answer_text: Local poles can exist due to magnetised mineral deposits.
parts.final_answer: Thus, local poles can exist on the earth's surface.

difficulty_reasoning: Requires understanding of magnetic concepts and their implications.

question_text:
Answer the following questions:
(a) The earth’s magnetic field varies from point to point in space. Does it also change with time? If so, on what time scale does it change appreciably?
(b) The earth’s core is known to contain iron. Yet geologists do not regard this as a source of the earth’s magnetism. Why?
(c) The charged currents in the outer conducting regions of the earth’s core are thought to be responsible for earth’s magnetism. What might be the ‘battery’ (i.e., the source of energy) to sustain these currents?
(d) The earth may have even reversed the direction of its field several times during its history of 4 to 5 billion years. How can geologists know about the earth’s field in such distant past?

mcq_options.option_text: The earth’s magnetic field varies from point to point in space. Does it also change with time? If so, on what time scale does it change appreciably?\n
The earth’s core is known to contain iron. Yet geologists do not regard this as a source of the earth’s magnetism. Why?\n

The charged currents in the outer conducting regions of the earth’s core are thought to be responsible for earth’s magnetism. What might be the ‘battery’ (i.e., the source of energy) to sustain these currents?\n
The earth may have even reversed the direction of its field several times during its history of 4 to 5 billion years. How can geologists know about the earth’s field in such distant past?

question_image.description: Images related to the magnetic field and its properties.

parts.part_text: Earth’s magnetic field changes with time. It takes a few hundred years to change by an appreciable amount. The variation in earth’s magnetic field with the time cannot be neglected.
parts.answer_text: Yes, the earth's magnetic field changes with time on a scale of a few hundred years.
parts.final_answer: Thus, it changes appreciably over a few hundred years.

parts.part_text: Earth’s core contains molten iron. This form of iron is not ferromagnetic. Hence, this is not considered as a source of earth’s magnetism.
parts.answer_text: The molten iron in the earth's core is not ferromagnetic, thus not a source of magnetism.
parts.final_answer: Therefore, the core's iron does not contribute to earth's magnetism.

parts.part_text: Radioactivity in earth’s interior is the source of energy that sustains the currents in the outer conducting regions of earth’s core. These charged currents are considered to be responsible for earth’s magnetism.
parts.answer_text: Radioactivity in the earth's interior sustains the currents responsible for magnetism.
parts.final_answer: Thus, radioactivity is the energy source for these currents.

parts.part_text: Earth reversed the direction of its field several times during its history of 4 to 5 billion years. These magnetic fields got weakly recorded in rocks during their solidification. One can get clues about the geomagnetic history from the analysis of this rock magnetism.
parts.answer_text: Geologists analyze rock magnetism to understand the earth's magnetic history.
parts.final_answer: Thus, rock analysis provides insights into the past magnetic fields.

difficulty_reasoning: Requires understanding of geological and magnetic concepts.

question_text: Answer the following questions: (a) Why does a paramagnetic sample display greater magnetisation (for the same magnetising field) when cooled? (b) Why is diamagnetism, in contrast, almost independent of temperature?

mcq_options.option_text: Why does a paramagnetic sample display greater magnetisation (for the same magnetising field) when cooled?
Why is diamagnetism, in contrast, almost independent of temperature?

question_image.description: Image related to magnetic fields and their inclination.

parts.part_text: Why does a paramagnetic sample display greater magnetisation (for the same magnetising field) when cooled?
parts.answer_text: Owing to the random thermal motion of molecules, the alignments of dipoles get disrupted at high temperatures. On cooling, this disruption is reduced. Hence, a paramagnetic sample displays greater magnetisation when cooled.
parts.final_answer: Thus, cooling enhances the magnetisation of a paramagnetic sample.

parts.part_text: Why is diamagnetism, in contrast, almost independent of temperature?
parts.answer_text: The induced dipole moment in a diamagnetic substance is always opposite to the magnetising field. Hence, the internal motion of the atoms (which is related to the temperature) does not affect the diamagnetism of a material.
parts.final_answer: Therefore, diamagnetism remains nearly constant regardless of temperature.

difficulty_reasoning: Requires understanding of magnetic properties and their temperature dependence.
